entities.summary: John II of Castile was King of Castile and León from 1406 to 1454, succeeding his older sister, Maria of Castile, Queen of Aragon, as Prince of Asturias in 1405. He played a crucial role in the Reconquista, a centuries-long campaign to reclaim the Iberian Peninsula from Moorish rule. John II's reign was marked by the rise of the Spanish Empire, with his court attracting scholars, artists, and intellectuals from across Europe. He also oversaw the construction of the Royal Monastery of Santa María la Real de El Escorial, a testament to his enduring legacy in Spanish history. The passing of John II in 1454 marked the beginning of a new era in Castile, as his nephew, Enrique IV, ascended to the throne, paving the way for the Habsburg dynasty's dominance in Spain. Despite his relatively short reign, John II's impact on the development of the Spanish Empire and the Iberian Peninsula's cultural heritage continues to be felt today. The 1454 Treaty of Alcalá, which ended the Reconquista, bears witness to his diplomatic prowess and commitment to his people's interests. Through his diplomatic efforts, John II secured crucial alliances with neighboring kingdoms, solidifying Castile's position as a major power in medieval Europe. John II of Castile's reign, though brief, left an indelible mark on Spanish history, cementing his place as one of the most important monarchs in the country's storied past. The succession of John II to the throne in 1406 marked a significant turning point in Castile's history, as he navigated the complex web of alliances and rivalries that defined medieval European politics. John II's reign was marked by periods of relative stability and prosperity, as well as episodes of conflict and turmoil, but his leadership and vision helped to shape the course of Castile's future.
